prompt: Which of the following claims is most consistent with Scientist 2's viewpoint?

choices.text: Comets contain very little frozen water.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says comets contain large amounts of frozen water.

choices.text: Any atmosphere the planet had soon after forming was lost to space.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 2 says the planet formed too hot to hold gases, so an early atmosphere would have escaped.

choices.text: Volcanic gases built most of the atmosphere over millions of years.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 1's view; Scientist 2 says volcanoes only recycle delivered material.

choices.text: The planet's argon isotope ratio points to a source inside the planet.
choices.rationale: The argon argument belongs to Scientist 1.

explanation: Scientist 2's reasoning begins with the loss of any original atmosphere, which is why delivery from space is needed.

stimulus.title: Where an Atmosphere Comes From
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
A rocky planet's atmosphere comes mainly from inside the planet. As the young planet's interior heated, volcanoes released water vapor, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen that had been trapped in its rocks. Over millions of years this outgassing built up a thick atmosphere. The mix of gases in such atmospheres closely matches the gases released by volcanoes today, and the ratio of certain forms of argon, called isotopes, points to a source within the planet rather than from space. Impacts by comets may have added small amounts of water, but the bulk of the atmosphere came from the planet's own interior.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The atmosphere was delivered mostly by comets and icy asteroids that struck the planet during the first several hundred million years after it formed. The planet formed too hot to hold onto gases; any early atmosphere would have been lost to space. Comets contain large amounts of frozen water and other ices, and the cratering record shows that impacts were extremely frequent during that early period. The ratio of heavy hydrogen, called deuterium, to ordinary hydrogen in the planet's water is similar to that measured in some comets. Volcanoes have released gases since, but they recycle material that impacts delivered rather than creating a new atmosphere.

prompt: Scientist 1 and Scientist 2 would both most likely agree that:

choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 makes this claim.

choices.text: the city's food supply declined before the city was abandoned.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 cites failed crops; Scientist 2 cites shrinking harvests. Both describe a failing food supply.

choices.text: the people of the city moved to river valleys when they left.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 1 says where the people went.

choices.text: rainfall in the region dropped sharply for more than a century.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 1 asserts the century-long drought; Scientist 2 allows only that a drought may have added strain.

explanation: Both explanations end with failing crops; they differ on why the crops failed.

stimulus.title: Why the City Was Abandoned
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The ancient city was abandoned because of a long drought. Layers of lake sediment from the region show a sharp drop in rainfall lasting more than a century, beginning just before the city's population began to fall. The city depended on reservoirs filled by seasonal rains, and excavations show the reservoirs were enlarged twice late in the city's history, a sign that water was becoming scarce. Tree-ring records from the surrounding hills confirm several decades of poor growth in the same period. Without reliable water, crops failed, and the people left for river valleys where farming remained possible.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The city was undone by its own irrigation. For centuries farmers watered their fields from canals, and in a hot climate much of that water evaporated, leaving behind the salts it carried. Soil samples from the old fields contain salt levels far too high for wheat, the city's main crop, and pollen records show a late shift toward barley, which tolerates salt better. Written tablets from the final decades record shrinking harvests on fields that still received water. A drought may have added to the strain, but the fields were already failing from salt before the dry period, and no amount of rain would have washed it away quickly.

prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strongly support Scientist 2's viewpoint?

choices.text: Traps on the ridge caught ten times as many beetles this year as they did five years ago.
choices.rationale: Beetle numbers support Scientist 1.

choices.text: Every dead tree examined contained beetle larvae galleries.
choices.rationale: Galleries show beetles were present, which both accept.

choices.text: Ridge pines given extra water in summer survived beetle attacks at the same rate as lower-slope trees.
choices.rationale: Correct. If water alone restores resistance, water shortage is what made the trees vulnerable.

choices.text: Beetles on the ridge now produce two generations each summer instead of one because winters are warmer.
choices.rationale: Extra generations support Scientist 1's view of the outbreak.

explanation: Scientist 2's claim is that drought removes the trees' defenses; restoring water and restoring survival shows that directly.

stimulus.title: The Dying Pines
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pines on the ridge are dying because of bark beetles. The beetles bore through the bark and lay eggs, and their larvae eat the living layer beneath, cutting off the flow of water and sugar. Every dead tree examined shows the winding galleries the larvae leave, and traps caught ten times more beetles this year than five years ago. Warm winters now let the beetles survive and produce two generations in a summer instead of one. Healthy trees can drown attacking beetles in resin, but a mass attack overwhelms even vigorous trees. Removing infested trees before the beetles emerge is the way to protect the rest of the stand.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The underlying cause is drought. Rainfall on the ridge has been below average for six of the past eight years, and the soil there is thin and holds little water. A tree short of water cannot make enough resin to repel beetles, so the insects succeed on trees that would normally resist them. Trees on the well-watered lower slopes carry the same beetles yet remain mostly alive, and tree rings from the dead pines show narrow growth for several years before the beetles arrived. Beetles are the final blow, not the cause. Unless the drought ends or the stand is thinned so that fewer trees compete for water, removing infested trees will not save the others.

prompt: Suppose researchers removed all magnetite from a group of bees and found that, on sunny days, these bees returned to the hive from unfamiliar locations just as well as untreated bees. This finding would most likely:

choices.text: weaken Scientist 2's viewpoint.
choices.rationale: Correct. If bees navigate normally without magnetite, the magnetic sense cannot be their main guide, at least when the sun is available.

choices.text: support both viewpoints equally.
choices.rationale: The finding favors the sun-compass view.

choices.text: support Scientist 2's viewpoint.
choices.rationale: Losing magnetite without losing navigation argues against the magnetic explanation.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 1's viewpoint.
choices.rationale: Normal navigation on sunny days is what the sun-compass view predicts.

explanation: Scientist 2 makes magnetite the key sensor; bees that navigate without it undercut that claim.

stimulus.title: How Bees Find Their Way
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Honeybees find their way home using the sun. A forager keeps track of the angle between its flight path and the sun, and it can read the pattern of polarized light in the sky even when the sun itself is hidden by clouds. Bees kept in the dark for several hours and then released set off in a direction shifted by the amount the sun has moved, showing that they steer by a remembered sun position. On fully overcast days with no polarized light, foragers often fail to return. Bees are also known to communicate the direction of food relative to the sun, which would be pointless unless the sun were their compass.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Bees rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field. Bees contain tiny grains of magnetite, an iron mineral that responds to magnetic fields, in their abdomens. In experiments, bees trained to find sugar water in one direction lost the ability when a small magnet was attached to them, and hives placed between strong electrical coils that disturbed the field produced disorganized combs. The sun is useful, but it moves across the sky and disappears at night and on cloudy days, so a fixed magnetic reference is needed. Bees that return home on overcast days are using the field, not the sky.

choices.text: whether the planet has ever had active volcanoes releasing gases.
choices.rationale: Both passages mention volcanoes.

choices.rationale: Correct. Both name an environmental catastrophe (impact or eruptions); neither considers biological causes such as competition.

stimulus.title: The End of the Dinosaurs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Earth 66 million years ago. The impact threw enormous amounts of dust and sulfur into the air, which blocked sunlight for months. Plants died, and the animals that depended on them starved. The clearest evidence is a thin layer of clay found at sites around the world that is rich in iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The layer sits exactly at the boundary where dinosaur fossils stop appearing. A crater of the right age and size has also been identified beneath the coast of Mexico. Because the layer and the crater are the same age, the impact must have been the main cause of the extinction.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India were the main cause. These eruptions released lava over an area larger than many countries and continued for hundreds of thousands of years. They poured carbon dioxide and sulfur gases into the atmosphere, causing rapid swings in climate and acid rain. Fossil records show that some groups of animals were already declining before the boundary layer formed, which an instant impact cannot explain. Iridium can also be carried up from deep within the Earth by such eruptions. An asteroid may have struck near the end, but it hit a world whose ecosystems were already collapsing from volcanic activity.

prompt: Both scientists would most likely agree that:

choices.text: weekday traffic is what drives the temperature difference.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 cites weekday traffic.

choices.text: painting roofs white would be the most effective remedy.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 explicitly says roof color changes would do less than reducing energy use.

choices.text: the extra warmth comes from sunlight stored in building materials.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 1 makes stored sunlight the cause.

choices.text: the city center is warmer than the countryside at night.
choices.rationale: Correct. Both passages set out to explain the same nighttime temperature difference.

explanation: The observation being explained, a warmer city at night, is shared; the cause is disputed.

stimulus.title: The Warm City
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The city center is about 4°C warmer at night than the surrounding farmland because of what the city is made of. Asphalt, brick, and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and store the heat, releasing it slowly after sunset. These surfaces are also dark, so they reflect less sunlight than fields and forests do. Vegetation cools the air as water evaporates from leaves, but the city has replaced most plants with pavement. The temperature difference is largest on clear, calm summer nights, when stored heat is released most effectively, and smallest in winter, when the sun is weak. Painting roofs white and planting trees would reduce the difference.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The warmth comes mainly from the energy people use. Every engine, air conditioner, furnace, and light releases heat into the city's air. In the dense center, this waste heat per square kilometer can rival the energy delivered by sunlight. The nighttime difference is large because the city keeps releasing heat after the sun sets, while the countryside does not. The difference also grows on weekdays, when traffic and business activity are heaviest, and shrinks on holidays, something that building materials alone cannot explain. Reducing energy use and improving the efficiency of vehicles and buildings would do more than changing roof colors.

prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strongly support Scientist 2's viewpoint?

choices.text: The nighttime temperature difference became much smaller during a week-long power outage.
choices.rationale: Correct. Less energy use with the same buildings leading to a smaller difference points to waste heat as the cause.

choices.text: Dark roofs are measured to be hotter than light-colored roofs at sunset.
choices.rationale: Hot dark roofs support the materials explanation.

choices.text: The temperature difference is largest on clear, calm summer nights and smallest in winter.
choices.rationale: This pattern is what Scientist 1 predicts from stored sunlight.

choices.text: Tree-lined streets are cooler at night than streets without trees.
choices.rationale: Cooling by trees supports Scientist 1's emphasis on vegetation.

prompt: Suppose the scratches on the large stones were found to run in many different directions, and laboratory tests showed that similar scratches form when stones grind together in a strong river current. This finding would most likely:

choices.text: weaken Scientist 2's viewpoint.
choices.rationale: Correct. The scratches would no longer point specifically to ice, removing a key piece of Scientist 2's evidence.

choices.text: support Scientist 2's viewpoint.
choices.rationale: The finding undercuts rather than supports the ice interpretation.

choices.text: support both viewpoints equally.
choices.rationale: The finding favors the river explanation.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 1's viewpoint.
choices.rationale: Scratches explainable by river action are consistent with Scientist 1's view.

explanation: Scientist 2 uses the scratches as a sign of ice; if rivers produce them too, that evidence loses its force.

stimulus.title: The Pebble Layer
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pebble layer exposed in the quarry wall was laid down by a fast-flowing river. The pebbles are well rounded, which happens when stones tumble against each other in moving water over long distances. They are sorted by size, with coarse pebbles at the bottom grading up to sand, exactly what a river deposits as its current slows. Many pebbles lie tilted in the same direction, the way a current stacks flat stones against the flow. The layer is also lens-shaped, thick in the middle and thinning to the sides, which matches the shape of a river channel cut into the older rock beneath it.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The layer was deposited by a glacier and the meltwater streams that flowed from it. Beneath the pebbles is a bed of unsorted material containing clay, sand, and boulders mixed together, a mixture that only ice can carry and drop in one place. Several of the larger stones have flat faces with parallel scratches, which form when stones are dragged along beneath moving ice. The pebbles above could have been rounded in meltwater streams at the glacier's edge, where sorting and tilting also occur over short distances. The region's climate records show it was cold enough for ice at the time, while river deposits need no such conditions.

choices.text: whether the Moon's iron core is small compared with the cores of other rocky bodies.
choices.rationale: Both describe a small core.

choices.text: whether the Moon currently orbits the Earth in a tilted orbit.
choices.rationale: Both accept that the Moon orbits Earth.

choices.text: whether the Earth itself has a large core made of iron.
choices.rationale: Both passages take Earth's iron core for granted.

choices.text: whether the Moon was built from Earth material or captured from elsewhere.
choices.rationale: Correct. Formation from Earth debris versus capture of a separate body is the central dispute.

explanation: The disagreement is about origin, not about the Moon's present features.

stimulus.title: The Origin of the Moon
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The Moon formed when a body about the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The collision blasted molten rock from Earth's outer layers into orbit, where it quickly gathered into the Moon. This explains why the Moon's rocks match Earth's in the ratios of oxygen isotopes, which differ from one body to another in the solar system. It also explains why the Moon has a very small iron core: the impact stripped mostly rocky material from the outside of the Earth, leaving Earth's iron core behind. The Moon's rocks are also unusually dry, as expected if they were once heated enough to drive off their water.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The Moon formed elsewhere in the solar system and was captured by Earth's gravity as it passed nearby. Capture explains why the Moon is so large compared with Earth; the impact scenario should have left a much smaller moon or none at all, as computer models of similar collisions often show. The matching oxygen isotopes could result from the Moon forming in the same region of the solar system as Earth, from the same raw material. A capture would have left the Moon in a tilted orbit, and the Moon's orbit is indeed tilted relative to Earth's equator. The small core could simply reflect the Moon's original composition.

choices.text: surface water and deep water are always the same temperature.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 relies on a temperature difference.

choices.text: plankton can see the fish that hunt them.
choices.rationale: Neither scientist discusses what plankton can see.

choices.text: the daily migration benefits the plankton that perform it.
choices.rationale: Correct. Each scientist proposes a benefit, safety or efficiency, and neither considers that the behavior might be useless or harmful.

choices.text: fish are the only predators that eat zooplankton.
choices.rationale: Neither scientist claims fish are the only predators.

explanation: Both treat the migration as an adaptation with a payoff; they differ only on what the payoff is.

stimulus.title: The Nightly Rise of Plankton
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Tiny animals called zooplankton spend the day hundreds of meters below the surface and rise to feed near the top only after dark because they are hiding from predators. The fish that eat them hunt by sight, so a plankton animal near the sunlit surface in daytime is easily seen and eaten. In the dark depths it is nearly invisible. Experiments in large tanks show that plankton stay deeper when fish are present and rise earlier when fish are removed, even if the light is unchanged. In lakes with no fish, the daily migration is weak or absent. The pattern is a trade-off: the surface offers food, but only the night makes it safe.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The migration is a way of saving energy. Water near the surface is warm, and a cold-blooded animal's body uses up energy faster in warm water. By feeding briefly at the surface and then sinking into cold, deep water, a plankton animal digests its food while burning fuel slowly, so it grows faster on the same amount of food. Measurements show that plankton which migrate convert food into body mass more efficiently than those that remain at the surface. Predators may matter in some lakes, but the migration also occurs in the open ocean where visual predators are scarce, and it follows the daily cycle of light because light sets the animals' internal clock, not because light reveals them.

prompt: Which of the following discoveries, if made, would most seriously undermine Scientist 1's explanation?

choices.text: Fertilizer use on the upstream farms has doubled over the past decade.
choices.rationale: More fertilizer strengthens the runoff story.

choices.text: Oxygen near the lake bottom in August is too low for most fish species to survive for more than a few hours.
choices.rationale: Low bottom oxygen is Scientist 1's own evidence.

choices.text: Dead algae are decomposed by bacteria that consume dissolved oxygen.
choices.rationale: This is the mechanism Scientist 1 describes.

choices.text: Perch eggs and young fish are found only in shallow, well-oxygenated water, never near the bottom.
choices.rationale: Correct. If young perch never occupy the low-oxygen zone, that zone cannot be what kills them.

explanation: Scientist 1's mechanism requires young perch to be exposed to the low-oxygen water; evidence that they are not breaks it.

stimulus.title: The Perch of Miller Lake
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The decline of perch in Miller Lake began soon after the farms upstream expanded. Fertilizer washed into the lake by rain feeds algae, which bloom across the surface each summer. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Measurements taken in August show oxygen levels near the bottom of the lake that are too low for perch eggs and young fish to survive. Adult perch can move to shallower water, but their young cannot, so each year fewer fish reach adulthood. Reducing fertilizer runoff would allow the oxygen to recover and the perch population to rebuild.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The perch decline is due to the arrival of the zander, a predatory fish first recorded in Miller Lake eight years ago, probably released by anglers. Zander feed heavily on young perch, and their numbers have grown each year while the perch count has fallen. Low oxygen alone cannot explain the pattern: the lake had algae blooms for decades before perch began to decline, and nearby lakes with similar farms and blooms still have healthy perch populations but no zander. Stomach samples from zander in the lake contain mostly young perch. Removing zander by netting would allow the perch to recover even if the fertilizer runoff continued.
